## Simple explanation

CUDA is a platform and programming model that lets software run
parallel computations on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). Many
machine-learning frameworks use it to accelerate supported operations.

## Technical explanation

CUDA includes programming interfaces, compilers, runtime components, and
libraries for executing workloads on compatible NVIDIA GPUs. Machine
learning frameworks often dispatch tensor operations to GPU libraries,
while also requiring compatible drivers, runtime components, framework
builds, and hardware.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

GPU acceleration enables many model-training and inference workloads to
run faster. CUDA compatibility and GPU memory capacity influence
environment setup, performance, portability, and deployment choices.

## How it works

A host program launches parallel kernels on a GPU. Data is transferred or
made available to device memory, computations run across many threads,
and results are returned or used by subsequent GPU operations. Frameworks
often manage these details behind higher-level tensor APIs.

## Practical example

A deep-learning framework can place model parameters and image batches on
a CUDA-capable GPU, then execute supported matrix and convolution
operations there rather than on the CPU.

## Common misconceptions

- CUDA is specific to NVIDIA GPUs and is not the name for all GPU
  computing.
- Installing a CUDA toolkit alone does not guarantee that a framework can
  use the available GPU.
- GPU execution is not automatically faster for small workloads or
  workloads dominated by data transfer.
